title: Break, Move, Settle — Changing Land
standard: NGSS 4-ESS2-1 (use observations or measurements as evidence of weathering effects or erosion rates)
reading:
## Break, Move, Settle

After rain, a muddy stream crosses a path. Farther downhill, a fan of sand lies where the water spread out. Both places hold clues about how land changes.

**Weathering** breaks rock down or changes it where it is. Water can enter a crack. If that water freezes, it can push against the sides. Repeated freezing and thawing can help widen some cracks. Roots growing in cracks can also push on rock. Not every crack forms in the same way.

**Erosion** moves rock or soil from one place to another. Flowing water can carry loose grains. Wind can move dry sand. Moving ice can carry rock. Gravity can pull loose material downhill. Breaking and moving can happen together, but they name different processes.

The loose pieces are called **sediment**. Some are tiny; others are large. **Deposition** happens when moving sediment settles or is left behind. A stream that slows may drop some of its load. Different sizes can settle at different places.

A **slope** is a slant in the land. Steeper slopes can change how water moves, but slope is not the only factor. The amount of water, the soil, and plant cover also matter. **Runoff** is water moving over the land surface.

How can we test one idea? Build two small trays with the same amount and kind of soil. Set different slopes. Add equal water amounts at the same rate and place. Catch the runoff in cups. Repeat the test with fresh setups. Decide how you will measure moved soil before you start.

Your **evidence** is what you observed or measured. A darker cup may suggest more suspended soil, but color alone is not an exact mass. A **model** helps us study a process at a small scale. A tray cannot copy a whole hillside.

Use careful language in your claim. Say what happened in your test, not what must happen on every hill. A useful explanation connects the evidence to a process and names a limit of the model.

short: Explain how a grain can experience erosion and deposition.
Water can carry the grain away from one place, which is erosion, then leave it in a slower part of the stream, which is deposition.
Why is water color not an exact soil-mass measurement?
Color can depend on particle type, size, lighting, and concentration. A darker cup alone does not provide a measured mass of moved sediment.
faq: No. A storm or slide can move a lot at once. Small changes can also build over time.
Is weathering the same as weather?
No. Weather is the state of the air. Weathering is rock breaking down or changing in place.
Yes. Roots and plant cover can hold soil and change water flow. Their effect depends on the setup.
Does all sediment settle at once?
No. Grain size and water movement affect when and where material settles.
challenge: A school garden path loses soil during rain. Our class can compare small soil trays to study one factor before suggesting a change.
How does tray slope affect the sediment moved by equal water inputs in our model?
Keep soil type, amount, water volume, and pour rate alike. Change slope. Collect runoff. Repeat fresh setups and record the same measure each time.
Report the setup, repeated observations, a supported claim, and one reason a tray differs from a real hillside.
facts: Erosion moves material and deposition leaves it behind.
A fair comparison controls other important conditions.
memoryText: Break in place. Think of a root pushing a rock crack wider.
The rock changes where it is. This cue helps keep breaking apart distinct from moving away.
Move, then leave. Think of sand carried by a stream, then left on a bank.
The two parts show two processes. Moving sand is erosion. Sand left behind is deposition.
